8750: Infancy means the earliest, most undeveloped stage of something. That "something" can be a human life, or it can be anything else — a company, a technology, an idea, a movement. The word always points to a beginning that is fragile, new, and still growing.
Meaning 1: The Earliest Stage of a Human Life

In its most direct and literal sense, infancy refers to the period of a person's life right after birth — roughly from birth up to around 1 to 2 years of age, though in casual usage people sometimes stretch it to mean the first few years before a child can speak or think independently.

During infancy, a person is called an infant. An infant is completely helpless and dependent on others for everything — feeding, warmth, movement, protection. They cannot speak, cannot walk, and cannot take care of themselves in any way. It is the most vulnerable and dependent phase of a human life.

"The doctor monitored the child's health carefully during infancy."
"Many habits and emotional patterns are shaped during infancy."

Think of infancy as the time when a person exists but has almost no ability to act on the world around them. They are alive, but just barely beginning.
Meaning 2: The Very Early Stage of Anything (Figurative Use)

This is the meaning you will encounter far more often in modern English. Infancy is widely used to describe the early, undeveloped stage of anything — not just human life. This is called a figurative (or metaphorical) use, meaning the word is borrowed from its original human-life meaning and applied more broadly.

The logic is simple: just as a human infant is new, undeveloped, weak, and full of potential, any new thing — a technology, a field of science, an industry, a political movement — can also be described as being in its infancy.

"In the 1990s, the internet was still in its infancy."
"Artificial intelligence, though powerful today, was in its infancy just a few decades ago."
"The company is still in its infancy and has a long way to go before it becomes profitable."
"The field of modern psychology was in its infancy in the late 1800s."

When you say something is "in its infancy," you are saying:

  • It is new and just getting started.
  • It is not yet fully formed or mature.
  • It has a lot of room to grow, improve, and develop.
  • It may be promising, but it hasn't reached its full potential yet.

This phrase — "in its infancy" — is one of the most common and important expressions built from this word. Memorize it, and you'll recognize it everywhere.

In law, particularly in older legal writing and some formal legal systems today, infancy refers to the state of being a minor — that is, a person who has not yet reached the legal age of adulthood (typically 18 years old, though this varies by country and context).

This legal meaning is broader than the everyday one. A 15-year-old is legally still in a state of "infancy" in this context, even though in everyday speech we would never call a teenager an infant.

In legal writing, you might see:

"The contract was void because one party was in a state of infancy at the time of signing."

This simply means the person was under the legal age of adulthood and therefore could not be legally bound by a contract. You won't encounter this meaning in everyday conversation, but it's good to know it exists so you're not confused if you ever read it in a legal document.
The Single Most Important Phrase to Know

If you remember nothing else, remember this:

"In its infancy"

This phrase means: at a very early, undeveloped stage. It is used all the time in journalism, academic writing, business, technology writing, and everyday conversation. Almost any time you see the word "infancy," it will appear inside this phrase.

"Infancy" is generally a neutral-to-positive word. It does not imply failure or weakness in a harsh way. Instead, it acknowledges that something is young and undeveloped while also hinting at future potential. When someone says a technology is "in its infancy," they are not insulting it — they are simply saying it is early, and the best is possibly yet to come.

ContextWhat "infancy" means

To pull it all together: infancy as a noun means the earliest, most undeveloped stage — of a human life (roughly birth to age 1–2), of anything new and not yet mature (figurative use), or of being legally under the age of adulthood (legal use). The figurative use is by far the most common in modern English, and the phrase "in its infancy" is the form you will see most often. The word always carries the idea of newness, fragility, potential, and incompleteness.
8751:
An infant is a very young child, typically from the moment of birth up to about one year of age, though in some contexts the word stretches to include children up to two years old.

Think of it this way: the moment a baby is born, it is an infant. As it grows, learns to walk, and starts talking in simple words, it gradually moves out of the "infant" stage and into being called a toddler.

An infant is defined not just by age, but by a cluster of characteristics that come with that stage of life:

  • Complete helplessness. An infant cannot feed itself, move around on its own, or do anything independently. It fully depends on adults for every single need — food, warmth, cleanliness, and safety.
  • Rapid development. During the infant stage, a human being grows and changes faster than at any other point in life. In just 12 months, a child goes from being unable to hold up its own head to attempting its first steps.
  • Pre-verbal communication. Infants cannot use words to express themselves. They communicate entirely through crying, facial expressions, and body movements.

This is where many learners get confused, so pay close attention.

  • Newborn — A newborn is a baby in its very first days or weeks of life (usually the first 28 days after birth). Every newborn is an infant, but not every infant is a newborn. "Newborn" is a more specific, narrower term.
  • Baby — "Baby" and "infant" are very close in meaning and are often used interchangeably in everyday speech. However, "baby" is the warmer, more informal and affectionate word. "Infant" is slightly more formal and clinical. A doctor will more likely say "infant"; a parent will more likely say "baby." Also, people sometimes call toddlers or even older children "baby" out of affection, while "infant" stays more strictly tied to the very young age range.
  • Toddler — A toddler is a child who has just begun to walk (usually ages 1–3). The word comes from the unsteady, "toddling" walk of a child just learning to use its legs. A toddler is older and more capable than an infant.
  • Child — "Child" is a broad word that covers everyone from birth all the way to adolescence. An infant is a child, but a child is not necessarily an infant.
How the Meaning Changes Depending on Context

The word "infant" is interesting because its precise meaning shifts slightly depending on where it is used.

In everyday conversation, an infant is simply a very young baby — most people picture a child under one year old.

In medicine and healthcare, "infant" usually means a child from birth to 12 months of age. You will often see phrases like infant mortality (the rate at which babies die before their first birthday) or infant formula (specially made milk for babies who are not breastfed).

In law (especially in older legal writing), "infant" has historically been used to mean any person who is under the legal age of adulthood — that is, anyone under 18. This legal meaning is largely old-fashioned today and rarely used in modern speech, but you might encounter it in older legal documents or literature. When you see it used this way, it simply means a legal minor, not a baby.

In the British education system, "infant school" refers to school for young children roughly aged 4 to 7. This is a local, specific use of the word within a particular educational tradition.

• Infant mortality — the death of a child before the age of one; used in public health discussions.
  • Infant formula — a manufactured substitute for breast milk.
  • Infant school — (mainly in the UK) a school for very young children.
  • Infant care — the general care and looking after of babies.
  • In its infancy — this is a figurative/metaphorical phrase, meaning something is in its earliest, least developed stage. For example: "Artificial intelligence was in its infancy in the 1980s." Here, "infancy" is borrowed from the image of a helpless infant to describe something that has barely begun.
The Tone and Register of the Word

"Infant" carries a tone of seriousness, formality, and precision. You will find it more in medical reports, academic writing, news articles, and official documents than in casual conversation. When parents talk about their own child at home, they say "my baby." When a pediatrician writes in a report, they are more likely to write "the infant."

This does not mean "infant" is cold or impersonal — it simply belongs to a slightly more formal register of language.

An infant is a very young human being, from birth to roughly one year of age (sometimes up to two), who is completely dependent on others, cannot speak, and is in the fastest developmental phase of human life. The word is more formal than "baby," more general than "newborn," and marks an earlier stage than "toddler." Its meaning can stretch in legal or educational contexts, but at its heart, it always points to the idea of the very beginning of life — small, vulnerable, and entirely new to the world.
8752: Infanticide means the deliberate killing of a very young child — almost always a newborn or a baby in the earliest months of life. The word has two related meanings in its noun form: it refers to the act itself (the killing), and less commonly, it can also refer to the person who commits the act. In everyday use, the first meaning — the act — is by far the more common one.

An infant, in the context of this word, is generally a baby from the moment of birth up to about one year of age. However, in most real-world cases — historical, legal, and social — infanticide refers most often to newborns, meaning babies killed within hours or days of being born. The younger the child, the more commonly the word applies.

It is important to understand that "infanticide" refers to killing after birth. It is a completely separate concept from abortion, which involves ending a pregnancy before birth. The two must not be confused.

When a baby is killed specifically within the first 24 hours of being born, there is an even more precise word for it: neonaticide (from "neonate," meaning newborn). Neonaticide is a type of infanticide, but infanticide is the broader term that covers the killing of a baby from birth through infancy.
Why Has Infanticide Happened Throughout History?

This is a deeply uncomfortable truth: infanticide has existed in virtually every major civilization throughout human history. Understanding the reasons why does not excuse it — but understanding it is essential to fully grasping what the word means and represents.

Economic hardship was one of the most common reasons. In societies where food was scarce, a family that simply could not feed another mouth might kill a newborn to ensure the survival of the children already alive. This was a tragic and brutal form of resource management.

Gender preference has been another major driver, particularly in cultures that valued sons far more than daughters. Female infanticide — the killing of baby girls specifically — has been widespread in parts of ancient and historical China, India, ancient Greece, Rome, and the Arab world before Islam. The reasons included the fact that daughters were seen as an economic burden (particularly in societies with expensive dowry systems), while sons were expected to carry the family name, inherit property, and support parents in old age.

Disability or physical difference was another reason. In ancient Sparta, for example, elders would inspect newborns, and those judged to be weak or unfit were abandoned to die. The logic, cold and brutal, was that the community could not afford to raise children who would not become strong soldiers or capable citizens.

Social stigma around illegitimacy — meaning children born outside of marriage — was also a powerful force throughout history. Women who gave birth to children they could not publicly acknowledge (due to shame, abandonment by a partner, or strict social rules) sometimes killed their babies to avoid disgrace or punishment.

Mental illness in the mother, particularly severe conditions triggered or worsened by the trauma of childbirth, has also been recognized as a cause. This does not make the act acceptable, but it does mean not all cases involve a cold, calculated decision.

The word is also used in biology and zoology to describe the killing of young by members of the same species in the animal world. For example, when a new male lion takes over a pride, he often kills the cubs fathered by the previous male. This behavior — also called infanticide — is well-documented across many species, including primates, rodents, and insects. In animals, it tends to occur for evolutionary reasons: a female whose offspring are killed will become ready to mate sooner, and the new dominant male can then pass on his own genes.

So when you see "infanticide" in a biology or nature context, it carries the same core meaning — killing of the young — but applied to non-human animals.

In all modern legal systems around the world, infanticide is a serious crime. It falls under the broader categories of murder or manslaughter. However, some countries have created specific laws around it that recognize the complex circumstances that may surround it.

The United Kingdom, for instance, has an Infanticide Act, which allows courts to treat a mother who kills her infant differently from a typical murder case — specifically when she was suffering from a severely disturbed mental state caused by the physical and psychological effects of giving birth or breastfeeding. In such cases, she may be convicted of "infanticide" as a specific, lesser charge rather than murder, and may receive treatment rather than a long prison sentence. This legal distinction reflects a compassionate recognition that severe postpartum mental illness can sometimes strip a person of rational judgment.

Most other countries, while not having this specific law, also take mental illness into account during sentencing in infanticide cases.

While infanticide is illegal everywhere today and is widely condemned morally and socially, it has not disappeared entirely.

Female infanticide still occurs in some parts of the world, particularly in rural regions of countries where strong son-preference cultures persist. In China, the now-abolished one-child policy (which restricted most families to having a single child) led, in some cases, to female infanticide or the abandonment of baby girls, because families desperately wanted their one allowed child to be a son.

Poverty-driven infanticide still surfaces in the most desperate corners of the world, though it is far rarer than in earlier centuries.

Mental illness remains a genuine factor in some modern cases, where a mother suffering from severe postpartum psychosis (a rare but serious mental condition after childbirth) may harm or kill her baby while in a state of crisis.

Infanticide also appears in academic philosophy and ethics as a subject of intellectual debate. A small number of philosophers have argued that newborns, lacking developed self-awareness or the ability to imagine their own future, do not yet hold the same moral status as older humans — and that infanticide might therefore be ethically different from killing an older person. This is an extreme and highly controversial position, rejected by the vast majority of ethicists, legal systems, and moral traditions worldwide. It is worth knowing this debate exists in philosophy, but it represents a fringe academic view, not a mainstream one.

Infanticide is a word that names one of the most tragic and disturbing acts possible: the killing of a baby. It is ancient, it is cross-cultural, it is illegal, and it carries enormous moral weight. It can refer to the act in human society or in the animal world. It can be driven by poverty, gender bias, mental illness, social shame, or cultural tradition — none of which make it permissible under modern law or widely accepted ethics, but all of which help explain how and why it has existed throughout human history.

Understanding this word fully means understanding not just its definition, but the painful human (and animal) realities that surround it.
8753:
An infant is a baby — a very young child who cannot yet speak, reason, or control their emotions and behavior. They cry when upset, throw things, demand immediate attention, and have no patience or self-control. That is simply their nature at that age, and it is perfectly normal.

Infantile means of, relating to, or resembling an infant or infancy.

But here is the important thing to understand: the word has two very different uses, and knowing both is key.

In scientific, medical, or clinical language, infantile simply means belonging to or occurring in infancy — with no judgment attached. It is purely descriptive.

  • Infantile reflexes — the automatic physical reflexes a newborn baby has, like gripping a finger placed in their palm.
  • Infantile amnesia — the well-known phenomenon where humans cannot remember events from the first two or three years of their life.
  • Infantile seizures — seizures that specifically occur in infants.

In this use, the word carries no insult or criticism. It is simply saying: "This thing belongs to the stage of life called infancy."
Use 2 — The Figurative, Critical Use (The Most Common Use)

This is where the word gets its real power, and this is almost certainly the use you will encounter most in daily life.

When you apply infantile to an adult's behavior, thoughts, or attitude, you are making a sharp criticism. You are saying that this person — who is old enough to know better — is behaving in a way that is so immature, so unreasonable, and so lacking in self-control that it resembles the behavior of a baby or a very young toddler.

Think about what makes a baby's behavior distinctly baby-like:

  • Throwing a tantrum the moment they don't get what they want
  • Refusing to share or cooperate
  • Being unable to handle any frustration, however small
  • Demanding constant attention
  • Acting entirely on impulse with zero self-reflection

When a grown adult does these things, you can call that behavior infantile. The word says: "You are acting like a baby, and that is deeply unbecoming of someone your age."

Examples in sentences:

  • "His infantile response to losing the argument — shouting and storming out of the room — shocked everyone present."
  • "She couldn't believe the infantile behavior on display when he simply refused to listen to any opinion other than his own."
  • "The politician's infantile name-calling during the debate made him look deeply unprofessional."
  • "Stop being infantile — just because things didn't go your way doesn't mean you get to sulk all day."

In every case, the word communicates strong disapproval. It does not just say someone is acting young — it says they are acting embarrassingly young for who they are and what is expected of them.

Infantile carries a tone of contempt, disappointment, and sharp criticism. It is not a gentle or kind word. When you call someone's behavior infantile, you are not playfully teasing them — you are making a serious, pointed judgment that their behavior is beneath them.

It is also a somewhat formal word. In casual speech, people might say "childish" or "babyish." But infantile feels stronger, more deliberate, and more cutting.

Understanding a word fully means knowing how it sits among words that look similar but are not quite the same.

Childish is the closest comparison. Something childish resembles the behavior of a child — a kid, say, aged 5 to 10. A childish argument might involve sulking, name-calling, or refusing to apologize. It is immature, but it still implies a child with some capacity for thought and language.

Infantile goes further. It implies behavior that is even more primitive — more like a screaming, helpless baby who cannot regulate a single emotion and has no reasoning ability whatsoever. So infantile is a stronger insult than childish. It digs deeper.

Juvenile and puerile are similar in meaning, but they are rarer words and infantile is far more commonly used.

Immature is the broadest of these words and the gentlest — it simply means "not fully developed or grown-up" and does not necessarily picture a baby in the way infantile does.
A Quick Mental Image to Remember This Word

Whenever you see or hear the word infantile applied to a person's behavior, picture a grown adult throwing a full baby tantrum — screaming on the floor, refusing to listen, completely unable to cope with not getting their way. That vivid image captures exactly what the word means when used critically.

The word is essentially saying: "This behavior belongs in a crib, not in an adult's life."

Infantile (adjective):

In its literal sense — relating to or characteristic of infants or infancy. Used mainly in medical and scientific language without any criticism.

In its figurative sense — describing the behavior, attitude, or thinking of an adult that is embarrassingly, contemptibly immature; so lacking in self-control, reason, or emotional maturity that it resembles the behavior of a baby. This is the dominant, everyday meaning and it carries a strong negative tone.
8754:
An infant is a very young baby or toddler — someone entirely dependent on others, emotionally reactive, physically underdeveloped, and mentally incapable of adult reasoning. Normally, these traits fade naturally as a person grows up.

Infantilism is the word we use when they don't — or when something that should be adult-level instead stays, reverts to, or resembles that early infant-stage. It is the condition of being infant-like where it does not belong.

The word is used in several distinct ways, and understanding all of them gives you full ownership of the word.

This is the most commonly encountered meaning. It refers to an adult who consistently thinks, feels, or acts like a child in ways that are inappropriate for their age.

This isn't just about being immature once in a while — everyone has moments like that. Infantilism, as a psychological concept, refers to a persistent, recurring pattern. Think of an adult who:

  • Has violent emotional meltdowns the moment something doesn't go their way (just like a toddler)
  • Is completely unable to tolerate frustration or delay gratification
  • Refuses to take responsibility for their actions, always blaming others
  • Demands that others make decisions for them and care for them as if they were a helpless child
  • Relies on extreme dependency on a parent, partner, or authority figure, well beyond what is healthy

A therapist or psychologist might describe such patterns in an adult client as infantilism — meaning their emotional and psychological development seems arrested (stuck) at an infant or very young child stage, even though their body has grown. It doesn't imply stupidity; it's specifically about emotional and behavioral development failing to keep pace with physical age.

In a clinical or medical context, infantilism refers specifically to a condition where a person's physical or mental development has been halted or severely delayed, leaving them with characteristics normally seen only in very young children, even as they grow older in years.

This can take different forms:

Physical infantilism means the body has not developed as expected. For example, a 16-year-old whose body still resembles that of a young child — no growth in height, no onset of puberty, no development of adult physical features. The body, in a sense, is "frozen" in an early stage of development. Historically, physicians used this term for various conditions involving stunted physical growth.

Sexual infantilism is a sub-category, referring specifically to the failure of sexual characteristics to develop normally — for example, the absence of puberty-related changes that would typically arrive in adolescence. This is a medical/endocrinological usage.

Mental infantilism refers to severe cognitive or intellectual development being arrested at an early childhood level, meaning the person's mental capacities remain those of a very young child throughout their life.

In all these medical cases, the key idea is the same: development stopped at an early, infant-like stage when it should have continued.

This is a recognized term in clinical psychology and psychiatry. Paraphilic infantilism (sometimes called adult baby syndrome, or abbreviated as AB/DL in informal communities) refers to a sexual paraphilia — an unusual pattern of sexual interest — in which an adult is sexually or emotionally aroused by pretending to be, or being treated as, an infant or very young baby.

This can involve wearing diapers, using baby bottles, wearing baby clothing, being "cared for" by someone playing the role of a parent, or other role-play that mimics infancy. The person is fully aware they are an adult; the behavior is chosen and role-played.

Clinically, it is only classified as a disorder if it causes significant distress to the person or harm to others. When it exists without causing distress or harm, it is simply referred to as a paraphilia (an atypical but not necessarily disordered variation in sexual interest).

Beyond psychology and medicine, "infantilism" is also used in intellectual, cultural, and political commentary to describe the tendency to treat people — or an entire society — as though they are children, or the tendency of a society to increasingly embrace child-like, shallow, or simplistic ways of engaging with the world.

There are two slightly different angles here:

Treating others as infants: When governments, corporations, media, or authority figures over-simplify everything, shield people from difficult truths, make all decisions "for people's own good" without allowing any independent judgment, or assume that ordinary people cannot handle complexity — critics call this infantilism. It's as if the powerful are saying, "You're a baby; let us handle the adult thinking." A political commentator might write: "This policy reflects the infantilism of the state — the assumption that citizens are incapable of making informed choices for themselves."

A society becoming infant-like: This usage describes a cultural drift where entertainment, politics, advertising, or public discourse becomes increasingly shallow, emotionally reactive, short-attention-spanned, and averse to nuance — mirroring the mental world of a small child. For example: "The infantilism of modern political debate — all slogans and outrage, no argument — is deeply worrying."

Every sense of "infantilism" connects back to the same central image: the infant — immature, undeveloped, dependent, emotionally reactive, and incapable of adult functioning. The word "infantilism" names a condition where that stage of life appears — persistently and problematically — where it has no place being.

Whether it describes a grown adult throwing tantrums (psychological), a body that stopped developing (medical), a sexual attraction to baby-like role-play (paraphilic), or a society being treated like children (cultural) — the word always points to one thing: infancy, showing up where it shouldn't.
8755:
To infantilize someone means to treat them as if they are a child — even though they are not. It means you act toward them as if they are less intelligent, less capable, or less mature than they actually are. In doing so, you take away — or ignore — their ability to think, decide, and act for themselves.

The word comes from infant, meaning a very young child. When you infantilize someone, you mentally "turn them into an infant" in the way you treat them.
What It Looks Like in Practice

Infantilizing doesn't always look the same. It can be subtle or very obvious. Here are the most common forms:

Making decisions for them without asking.
You decide what's best for someone instead of letting them decide for themselves. You assume they can't figure it out, so you just handle it for them — without their input.

Over-explaining things they already know.
You break things down far more than necessary, as if they've never encountered a simple idea before. You explain things slowly, repeatedly, or in an overly basic way that would be appropriate for a child but feels insulting to an adult.

Using baby talk or an exaggerated, soft tone.
You speak to them in a voice or with words that you'd use for a toddler — overly cheerful, soft, slow, or simplified. This is common, for example, when some people speak to the elderly or to those with disabilities.

Withholding information "for their own good."
You decide they can't handle the truth, the full story, or the complexity of a situation, so you hide it, soften it beyond recognition, or give them a watered-down version. You become their gatekeeper rather than trusting them to process information themselves.

Overprotecting them.
You constantly step in to prevent them from facing any difficulty, risk, or discomfort — because you don't believe they're capable of handling it. This stops them from growing, learning, or taking any ownership of their own life.

Dismissing their opinions or feelings.
You treat their thoughts as not worth seriously engaging with — the way an adult might wave off a child's argument as "cute" rather than responding to it with real respect.

In a family:
A parent continues to manage every aspect of their 30-year-old child's life — booking their appointments, handling their finances, telling them what to eat. The parent may love their child deeply, but they are infantilizing them by never trusting them to be a capable adult.

In healthcare:
A doctor explains a diagnosis to a patient's family member instead of talking directly to the patient. Or a doctor uses a soothing, over-simplified tone with an elderly patient who is mentally sharp — just because of their age. The patient is being infantilized.

In the workplace:
A manager never gives an employee any real responsibility, checks every small decision they make, and explains instructions as if the employee has never done anything before — even though they're experienced. That employee is being infantilized.

In media and advertising:
When a company's advertisement assumes its audience can't understand anything complex and dumbs content down to an almost insulting degree, it is infantilizing its audience. Or when a government constantly tells citizens what they should think or feel rather than presenting them with honest information and trusting them to form their own conclusions.

In a relationship:
A partner constantly speaks on behalf of the other person in social situations, answers questions directed at them, and makes all the household decisions — treating the other person like a dependent rather than an equal. That is infantilization.
Why It Matters — The Harm It Causes

Infantilizing someone is harmful for several reasons:

It strips dignity. Every adult has a right to be treated as a capable person. When someone infantilizes you, they are signaling — whether they mean to or not — that they see you as less than fully competent. This is deeply disrespectful.

It removes autonomy. Autonomy means the ability to make your own choices. When someone infantilizes you, they take that away. Over time, this can make a person feel powerless, dependent, and unsure of themselves.

It can create the very helplessness it assumes. If someone is constantly treated as incapable, they may begin to become more dependent over time. The infantilization creates the condition it was supposedly responding to — a vicious cycle.

It breaks trust. Being infantilized sends a message: "I don't trust you." That feeling of not being trusted by someone close to you — a parent, a doctor, a boss — is painful and damaging to the relationship.

This is an important distinction.

Sometimes infantilization is deliberate — used as a tool of control or power. By treating someone like a child, you keep them dependent on you. You position yourself as the authority, the wise one, the one in charge.

But more often, infantilization is well-meaning. People infantilize others out of love, protectiveness, or habit — without realizing how it comes across. A parent who still treats their adult child like a helpless 8-year-old may genuinely just love them and want to help. A nurse who uses baby talk with elderly patients may think she's being warm and kind.

The good intentions do not cancel the harm. The impact on the other person — the feeling of not being trusted, not being respected, not being seen as a capable adult — is real, regardless of what the person doing it intended.

The word can also point inward. A person can infantilize themselves — meaning they voluntarily act more helpless, dependent, or immature than they actually are. This might look like:

  • Refusing to take responsibility for decisions
  • Always relying on others to solve problems they could handle themselves
  • Avoiding any situation that requires them to act like a capable adult

This is sometimes a response to having been infantilized for a long time — people can internalize the message that they aren't capable.

If you want one sentence to anchor this word in your memory: to be infantilized is to be treated as less than the capable adult you are. The person on the receiving end typically feels a mix of frustration, humiliation, and powerlessness — not because they are being attacked, but because they are being underestimated in a way that feels just as bad.

Understanding these nearby words will sharpen your understanding:

To patronize — to treat someone as if they are less intelligent or important than you, often while pretending to be helpful or kind. Infantilizing often is patronizing, but patronizing is a broader term.

To condescend — to speak or behave as though you are superior to someone. Closely related, but condescension is more about tone and attitude, while infantilizing is specifically about treating someone as a child.

To coddle — to treat someone too gently, protecting them from any hardship. Coddling is one of the most common forms of infantilizing.

To undermine — to weaken someone's confidence or authority. Infantilizing often results in undermining someone.

What it meansTo treat someone as if they are a child — less capable, less intelligent, or less mature than they actually are
Who it affectsAnyone: adults, the elderly, patients, employees, citizens, partners
How it shows upOver-explaining, deciding for others, withholding information, over-protecting, using baby talk
The core harmIt strips dignity and autonomy; it disrespects the person's full humanity
IntentOften well-meaning, but harmful regardless of intention
8756:
Infantry refers to the soldiers of an army who fight primarily on foot, and also to the branch of an army to which those soldiers belong.

Think of it this way: armies use many kinds of fighting forces — soldiers on horseback, soldiers in tanks, soldiers in aircraft, soldiers on warships. Infantry is specifically the group of soldiers whose main job is to walk, march, and fight on the ground, face to face with the enemy, using weapons they carry in their own hands, such as rifles, machine guns, and grenades.

A single soldier belonging to this group is called an infantryman (or infantrywoman). The whole group, as a unit or branch, is called the infantry.

Infantrymen are the fighters who physically move across land, close in on the enemy, and engage them directly. Their core tasks include:

  • Attacking enemy positions — moving toward the enemy and fighting to overpower them.
  • Defending positions — holding ground so the enemy cannot take it.
  • Patrolling — moving through an area to watch for threats, gather information, or maintain security.
  • Occupying territory — physically being present on land to control it.

This last point is one of the most important things to understand: no matter how powerful a military's bombs, missiles, drones, or tanks are, only infantry can truly occupy and hold ground. Technology can destroy; infantry controls. This is why infantry has been called "the queen of battle" — she may not always be the most dramatic piece on the chessboard, but she is the one who ultimately determines who wins.
How Infantry Differs from Other Military Forces

It helps to understand infantry by contrasting it with other forces:

  • Cavalry (historically) → soldiers who fight on horseback. Infantry fights on foot.
  • Armored forces / tank crews → soldiers who fight inside tanks or other armored vehicles. Infantry fights in the open, on foot.
  • Artillery → soldiers who operate large guns or missile systems that fire at enemies from a distance. Infantry fights up close.
  • Air force → soldiers who fight from aircraft. Infantry fights on the ground.
  • Navy → soldiers who fight from warships at sea. Infantry fights on land.

Infantry is the oldest and most fundamental of all these — armies have had foot soldiers since the very beginning of organized warfare.

Not all infantry is the same. Over time, armies have developed specialized kinds:

  • Light infantry — soldiers who travel fast with minimal equipment, ideal for difficult terrain like mountains or jungles where heavy vehicles cannot go.
  • Mechanized infantry — soldiers who ride into battle in armored vehicles (like armored personnel carriers or infantry fighting vehicles) but dismount and fight on foot. They get the speed and protection of vehicles, combined with the flexibility of foot soldiers.
  • Airborne infantry (paratroopers) — soldiers delivered to a battlefield by parachuting from aircraft or by helicopter, allowing them to appear suddenly behind enemy lines or in locations that would be hard to reach otherwise.
  • Marine infantry — soldiers trained to launch attacks from the sea onto land (called amphibious operations), arriving by ship and fighting their way onto shore.
  • Mountain / alpine infantry — soldiers specially trained and equipped to fight in steep, cold, high-altitude terrain.

Despite these differences, all of them share the defining quality: when the moment of battle comes, they get out and fight on foot.

Infantry is mostly used as an uncountable noun, meaning you typically don't say "an infantry" or "infantries." Instead, you use it to refer to the concept or to the group as a whole.

Some natural examples:

  • "The infantry advanced toward the ridge." — referring to the soldiers as a group.
  • "He served in the infantry for six years." — referring to the branch of the military.
  • "Infantry training is physically demanding." — referring to the concept of that type of soldiering.
  • "They called in infantry support." — referring to infantrymen being deployed for help.

When you want to refer to a single soldier from this group, you use infantryman or infantrywoman, not "an infantry."

You might wonder: in an age of drones, missiles, and stealth bombers, why do we still need soldiers walking around with rifles?

The answer is simple but profound: wars are ultimately won or lost over who controls the ground, and only human beings on foot can truly control it.

A missile can destroy a building. A tank can drive through a town. A drone can observe a hillside. But none of them can walk into a building, clear it room by room, talk to the people inside, guard a checkpoint, secure a neighborhood, or prevent an enemy combatant from hiding among civilians. Only infantry can do those things.

This is why, even in the most technologically advanced militaries in the world today, infantry remains the largest single group of soldiers and is considered the foundation of land warfare.

Infantry is the branch of an army made up of soldiers trained to fight on foot, and it refers both to those soldiers collectively and to the military branch itself — the oldest, most essential, and most numerous element of any land-based fighting force.
8757:
When you are infatuated with someone, you have an extremely intense, all-consuming feeling of attraction toward them — but one that is based more on how you imagine them to be, rather than who they truly are. Your feelings are so powerful that they cloud your thinking and judgment. You essentially lose your ability to see that person clearly or realistically.

Think of it this way: your mind gets so flooded with feelings for this person that it builds an almost perfect, idealized picture of them in your head — and you fall for that picture, not necessarily the real, full, complex human being.

There are four key qualities that make infatuation what it is:

1. The feelings are extremely intense.
This is not a mild "I kind of like this person." Being infatuated means you think about the person constantly, you feel a rush of excitement around them, and they occupy a huge space in your mind. It borders on obsession.

2. The feelings cloud your judgment.
When you are infatuated, you tend to ignore the person's flaws or weaknesses. Even if others around you can see those flaws clearly, you cannot — or you refuse to. You put this person on a pedestal.

3. The feelings are usually short-lived.
Infatuation tends to burn bright but fade. It's the kind of feeling that often cannot survive the test of time or deep knowledge of the person. Once you truly get to know someone — including their imperfections — the infatuation may wear off.

4. The feelings are based on surface-level knowledge.
You are usually infatuated with someone you don't know very well yet. You are drawn to how they look, how they carry themselves, one or two things they said, or simply the idea of them. There is little depth of real understanding behind the feeling.

This is the most important distinction to understand, and people confuse these two all the time.

Being infatuated is like standing outside a beautifully lit house at night, staring through the window, and imagining how perfect and wonderful life inside must be — based almost entirely on what you want to see.

Being in love is like actually living inside that house — knowing every creaky floorboard, every messy corner, every difficult morning — and choosing to stay anyway.

In short: infatuation is about a fantasy. Love is about reality.

Infatuation feels just as powerful as love, and it can even feel like love, especially when you are in the middle of it. But it is driven by imagination and idealization, not by genuine deep knowledge of another person.
Who or What Can You Be Infatuated With?

Most commonly, a person is infatuated with another person — a crush, a celebrity, someone they just met.

But the word can also be used more broadly. You can be infatuated with an idea, a hobby, a lifestyle, or even a place — when you are completely swept up in it in an uncritical, almost irrational way.

"Infatuated" carries a slightly cautionary tone. When someone says "you're just infatuated," they are gently suggesting that your feelings, while real and powerful, may not be grounded in reality. It is not an insult — the feeling itself is very human and extremely common — but it does imply that the feelings deserve a reality check.

These will show you how the word feels in real use:

  • "She was so infatuated with him that she couldn't see how poorly he treated her."
  • "I was infatuated with her from the moment I saw her, but once we actually spent time together, I realized we had nothing in common."
  • "He's not really in love — he's infatuated. Give it a few months and the feeling will pass."
  • "As a teenager, I was completely infatuated with the idea of becoming a rock star."
  • "She knew she was infatuated, not in love, because she loved the idea of him more than she actually knew him."

If you ever need to recall this word quickly, remember this:

Infatuated = so intensely attracted to someone that your feelings are overwhelming, your judgment is clouded, and you are more in love with your idea of them than with who they truly are.
8758:
Infatuation is an intense, overwhelming feeling of attraction or passion toward someone — but one that is based more on imagination and fantasy than on truly knowing that person. Think of it as a kind of emotional blindness: when you are infatuated with someone, your feelings are so strong and exciting that you see that person as almost perfect, even though you may barely know them at all.

The key word here is intense but shallow. It feels very real and very powerful from the inside, but it lacks the deep roots that genuine, lasting feelings are built on.

When someone experiences infatuation, they typically:

  • Think about the other person constantly — almost obsessively
  • Feel a rush of excitement whenever the person is nearby or even just mentioned
  • Idealize the person, meaning they see only the best qualities and ignore or fail to notice any flaws
  • Feel a desperate, urgent need to be close to or noticed by that person
  • Confuse this feeling with being "in love"

It's the emotional equivalent of being under a spell. Everything about that person seems magical and flawless. Your heart races. Your mind wanders to them constantly. It can feel like the most real thing you've ever experienced — and yet, it is largely a product of your own imagination projecting perfection onto another person.
The Most Important Distinction: Infatuation vs. Love

This is where understanding this word gets really rich. Infatuation is frequently mistaken for love, and understanding the difference is crucial.

InfatuationLove

Infatuation arrives suddenly, like a lightning bolt. Love grows gradually, over time, as you come to deeply know someone.

Infatuation is about how a person makes you feel — the thrill, the excitement, the rush. Love is about genuinely caring about the other person's wellbeing, even when it isn't thrilling or exciting.

Infatuation is built on an idealized image of someone — a version of them that you've constructed in your mind, which may not match who they really are. Love is built on real knowledge of a person, including their flaws, their bad days, and their imperfections — and choosing to care for them anyway.

Infatuation fades. Often quite quickly. Once you get to know the real person, or once time simply passes, the intense feeling dissolves. Love deepens with time rather than fading.

Infatuation tends to create anxiety and obsession — you're constantly wondering if they like you back, constantly craving their attention. Love tends to bring a sense of security, comfort, and peace.

A useful way to remember it: infatuation is a feeling about a fantasy; love is a feeling about a real person.
It Doesn't Only Apply to People

While infatuation is most commonly used in a romantic context, it can also apply to a passionate, short-lived obsession with a thing, an idea, a celebrity, or even a place. For example:

  • Someone who becomes absolutely obsessed with a new hobby for a few weeks, then drops it, might be described as having had an infatuation with it.
  • A fan who is completely consumed by admiration for a celebrity might be described as being infatuated with them.

This is important: infatuation carries a slightly skeptical or dismissive tone. When someone uses this word to describe your feelings, they are gently (or sometimes not so gently) suggesting that what you feel is not as deep or as lasting as you think it is. It implies that your feelings are intense but temporary, and perhaps not entirely based in reality.

Calling something an infatuation is often a way of saying: "This feels enormous right now, but it will pass."

Here are sentences that show the word being used naturally, so you can see exactly how it fits into real language:

  • "What he believed was love turned out to be a brief infatuation — within a month, his feelings had completely faded."
  • "Her infatuation with the new colleague made it impossible for her to think clearly at work."
  • "It's just an infatuation," her mother said gently. "You don't even know him yet."
  • "He had a teenage infatuation with a famous singer that he still laughs about today."
  • "The infatuation was mutual — they both couldn't stop thinking about each other — but neither of them really knew the other person at all."

• Infatuated (adjective) — the most common form you'll encounter. "She was completely infatuated with him." This means she was in the grip of infatuation.
  • Infatuate (verb) — less commonly used, but it means to cause someone to experience infatuation. "Her charm seemed to infatuate everyone she met."

These are word combinations that native speakers naturally use with infatuation:

  • A passing infatuation — one that comes and goes quickly
  • A brief infatuation — same idea; short-lived
  • A teenage infatuation — the kind of intense crush common in adolescence
  • Infatuation with someone/something — the standard preposition is with
  • Blind infatuation — emphasizing how it prevents you from seeing clearly

If you had to remember just one line:

Infatuation is an intense, blinding, and usually short-lived feeling of passion or attraction toward someone or something, based more on an idealized fantasy than on genuine knowledge.

Everything else in this explanation is simply unpacking the layers of that one idea. You now understand not just what the word means, but how it feels, how it differs from deeper emotions, how it's used in sentences, and what tone it carries — which means you understand it the way a native speaker does, not just as a dictionary definition.
8759: Infeasible means not able to be done or carried out in practice. When something is infeasible, it cannot be successfully achieved given real-world conditions — the barriers standing in the way (like cost, time, resources, technology, or logic) are simply too great to overcome.
The Key Idea Behind the Word

Think of any plan, idea, or task. For it to work, certain conditions need to be met — you need enough money, enough time, the right tools, the right people, and so on. When those conditions cannot realistically be met, the plan is infeasible — it just won't work in the real world.

"Building a hospital in three days is infeasible — there isn't enough time or workforce to make it happen."

The word is a judgment: someone has looked at what a task requires and concluded that it simply cannot be done the way things currently stand.
Infeasible vs. Impossible — A Critical Distinction

This is the most important nuance to understand about this word, and most learners miss it.

Impossible means something cannot happen at all — it defies the laws of nature, logic, or reality itself.

  • "It is impossible to travel back in time."

Infeasible means something could theoretically happen but cannot be done in practice given real constraints like money, time, technology, or effort.

  • "Sending a human to Mars next week is infeasible." (Not impossible — humans have gone to space — but the time, preparation, and resources needed make it unworkable right now.)

In short: impossible closes the door permanently. Infeasible means the door exists, but you currently can't get through it.

Infeasibility always has a reason — a real, practical barrier. Here are the most common causes:

1. Not enough money

"The proposed stadium renovation is financially infeasible — it would cost ten times the city's annual budget."

2. Not enough time

"Completing 500 pages of legal documents by tomorrow morning is infeasible."

3. Lacking the right technology

"In the 1950s, sending a message instantly across the world was considered infeasible."

4. Not enough people or resources

"With a team of two, finishing this construction project in a month is infeasible."

5. Logical or structural barriers

"The plan requires two things to happen simultaneously in different cities — that's infeasible with only one team."
How and Where the Word is Used

"Infeasible" is a formal word. You will mostly see it in:

  • Business and planning: "The board declared the merger infeasible after reviewing the financials."
  • Engineering and science: "The design was deemed infeasible due to material limitations."
  • Law and policy: "The proposed regulation was found to be infeasible to enforce."
  • Everyday formal speech: "Working two full-time jobs while studying is infeasible for most people."

In casual conversation, people tend to say "not doable," "not realistic," or "can't be done" instead — but in professional or academic settings, infeasible is the precise and preferred term.

The word almost always appears in these structures:

  • "It is infeasible to [do something]" → "It is infeasible to redesign the entire system in one week."
  • "[Something] is infeasible" → "The plan is infeasible."
  • "[Something] is infeasible given [condition]" → "The project is infeasible given our current budget."
  • "deemed / considered / found infeasible" → "The proposal was deemed infeasible by the committee."

You'll also see it modified to pinpoint what kind of infeasibility:

  • Technically infeasible — the technology doesn't exist or doesn't work well enough.
  • Financially infeasible — it costs more than what's available or reasonable.
  • Logistically infeasible — the coordination, movement, or organization required simply can't happen.
  • Practically infeasible — a broader term meaning it just won't work in the real world, even if no single specific reason dominates.

The opposite of infeasible is feasible, which means able to be done; workable; realistic. Understanding both words together makes each one sharper:

Feasible"We have the budget, time, and team — this is feasible."
Infeasible"We don't have the budget or the time — this is infeasible."

When someone conducts a "feasibility study," they are asking: Is this plan feasible, or is it infeasible? They examine the real-world conditions to decide whether the goal can actually be achieved.
Words Close in Meaning — and How They Differ

These words are related to "infeasible" but are not identical:

  • Impossible — Stronger. Cannot happen at all, ever. (Infeasible just means not workable right now or under current conditions.)
  • Impractical — Weaker. It can be done, but it's inconvenient, inefficient, or unwise. (Infeasible means it genuinely cannot be done, not just that it's a bad idea.)
  • Unworkable — Very close in meaning. Usually used for plans or systems that won't function as intended. (Slightly more informal than infeasible.)
  • Unrealistic — Close, but more about expectations being out of touch with reality. (Infeasible is more objective and grounded in specific, concrete barriers.)
  • Unachievable — Means the goal cannot be reached. (Similar to infeasible but slightly more about the end result than the process.)
A Few More Examples to Cement It

• "The teacher asked for a 10,000-word essay due in one hour. That's infeasible."
  • "It is infeasible to heat an entire city using a single small generator."
  • "Their business model was infeasible — they were spending three dollars for every dollar they earned."
  • "Scientists once thought flying was infeasible, until the Wright Brothers proved otherwise." (This last example beautifully shows that infeasibility is often temporary — tied to current conditions, not eternal truth.)

Infeasible means something cannot be done in practice because the real-world barriers — whether of money, time, technology, resources, or logic — are too great to overcome, even if the idea itself isn't outright impossible.
